title: Ullambana
hook: the Chinese festival of offering for ancestors, from Moggallana's mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rains retreat: a vow of place that bends for real need. Your line: stay in one place.

Paper slips cover a long wall in a Chinese temple hall, row after row, each with a name brushed onto it. Some names belong to the dead: a grandfather, a mother, a baby who didn't live long. Some belong to the living: a sick father, a child taking exams. In front of the wall, tables are heaped with fruit, rice, flowers and cloth. Monks file in and chant. This is the Ullambana assembly, held in the seventh lunar month. You've met its Japanese cousin, Obon, with its fires and dances. Today, stay in the Chinese hall, and ask why the wall holds the names of the living as well as the dead.
screen: `NAMES ON PAPER SLIPS.` → `THE DEAD AND THE LIVING.` → `WHY BOTH?`

segments.voice: First, the story, told a few days ago at the home altar. In the Ullambana Sutra, a Chinese Buddhist scripture, the disciple Moggallana finds his dead mother among the hungry ghosts and can't feed her himself. The Buddha sends him to give, on the day the monks finish their summer retreat, to the whole community of monks: food, bowls, bedding, the things they need. Then what the sutra does next, which is easy to miss. It doesn't stop with one mother. Moggallana asks whether other disciples, in times to come, could make the same offering for their own parents. The Buddha says yes, and widens it. Then the living. The sutra says the same offering helps parents who are still alive, bringing them long life and freedom from illness, and it reaches back through the generations of ancestors too. That's why the paper slips carry both kinds of names. Last, what the festival became. The sutra ends with the Buddha telling disciples who care for their parents to make this offering every year, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. In China and across East Asia, families still bring names and offerings to temples in that month. Some readers hear in it a festival about care that runs both ways in time: for the parents who are still here, and the ones who came before them.
screen: `HE CAN'T FEED HER HIMSELF.` · `GIVE TO THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `FOR THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.` · then, large: `FOR THE ANCESTORS.`

segments.voice: Let one parent or ancestor come to mind, living or gone, or, if no one in your family feels right, a teacher or someone who raised you; picture their face, or just their name. Think of one small thing you could offer to others in their name, groceries for a food bank, a meal for a neighbor, an hour of help, and rest with them as you breathe. If someone's absence weighs too much to hold alone, you can call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

howItsDone: In Chinese and other East Asian Buddhist communities, families bring offerings to temples in the seventh lunar month and register the names of deceased ancestors and living relatives, while monks chant the Ullambana assembly.

chat.says: Why are there names of living people on the wall at the Ullambana festival?
options: The sutra says the offering also helps living parents, with long life and good health.
Those families paid the temple for a place, so their names go up beside the dead.
It's a mistake; the festival is meant only for those who have already died.
chat.meaning: In the Ullambana Sutra, the Buddha widens Moggallana's offering: it helps living parents with long life and health, and reaches back through the ancestors.

Ullambana.meaning: the festival of offerings for ancestors and parents

notes: Ullambana Sutra paraphrased: Moggallana's food bursts into flame (not retold here); the Buddha says one person's power is not enough and directs offerings to the assembled sangha of the ten directions on the day they end the summer retreat (15th of the 7th month); the merit benefits present parents (long life, freedom from illness) and seven generations of ancestors.
